title: The women, closed
hookLine: founders, teachers, mothers, queens: the women of the first sangha, gathered up

cards: There's a book in the Pali canon made of women's voices: the Therigatha, the verses of the elder nuns.
In it, women speak in the first person about leaving home, about grief and children, about bodies and aging, and about the moment their minds were freed.

It sits beside the Theragatha, the monks' verses, in the same collection. Several of the women from the last two weeks speak there, in their own lines. For two weeks this path has followed them one at a time.
Today, gather them up, and see what they look like standing together.

teach.b: First, the founders. Mahapajapati, the Buddha's foster mother, who asked for women to go forth, was refused, asked again, and led the first women into the order.
Yasodhara, whom the commentaries remember as the nun Bhadda Kaccana, foremost in great higher knowledge, on a path of her own.
Second, the teachers. Khema, whose answer to King Pasenadi matched the Buddha's own. Dhammadinna, whose answers he said he would have given the same way.
Patacara, who drew the arrow of grief out of other mothers and was named foremost in the discipline.
Third, the mothers and survivors. Uppalavanna, foremost in psychic power, who survived harm and met Mara unafraid. Kisa Gotami, after the mustard seed, in rough robes with a clear mind.
Sona, mother of ten, who began late and was named foremost in energy.
Fourth, the givers and the queens. Ambapali, who kept the Buddha's meal against the princes and gave her mango grove. Visakha, a laywoman, with her father's riddles and her eight practical requests.
Mallika, the queen who heard a hard answer and resolved to give. What runs through them all? They aren't footnotes in someone else's story.
In the texts they get titles of their own, answers of their own to hard questions, and, in the Therigatha, words of their own. One answered a king. One kept the community's rules.
One heated the bath water and woke. Khema in a vision, and Ambapali in her verses, looked straight at aging.
The women of the first sangha learned, and they taught. She taught too.

how: The Therigatha is read in Theravada communities alongside the monks' verses, and the first nuns and laywomen are remembered by the titles the Buddha's list gives them.

o: the nuns who lived in the forest alone
the queens who ruled over Kosala's palace
the first sangha's founders, teachers and givers

p: led the first women into the order
the Buddha would have answered the same

s: the women of the first sangha appear only as side characters
the suttas name them foremost in their own qualities, and the Therigatha gives them their own verses.
one of these women woke while heating the bath water
Sona, the mother of ten who began late, named foremost in energy.
every woman in these two weeks became a nun

games.q: you're Mahapajapati. you've asked the Buddha to let women go forth, and he has refused. what do you do?
games.why: she was refused, asked again, and led the first women into the order.

practice: Let one woman come to mind who taught you something that stayed: a mother or grandmother, a teacher, an aunt, a writer you never met, maybe someone whose name no one else would know.
Say her name silently, and put what she taught you into one sentence. Hold her there a moment, the way the Therigatha holds these women's voices.

wordCard.voice: The women. Founders, teachers, mothers, survivors, givers and queens: the women of the first sangha. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali theri, an elder nun: the Therigatha is the verses of the theris.

carryVoice: Your line: she taught too. Their own words are still read today. Seven hundred sixty-six days now.
